belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

The first element is your business case. The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources.
reply.example:
Sample only — to show the form of a good answer. Do not copy it; answer for your own process.
During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

belt: Across our three hospital sites, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms from January to June 2026. Late payments to our suppliers are costing us: we paid about £62,000 in late-payment interest and lost early-payment discounts last year, and three key medical suppliers put us on stop twice this year, which held up ward stock.

reply.answer:
Your business case names what is going wrong, where and since when, and it explains the costs involved. However, it is missing a baseline value as a number — how big the problem is today, expressed as a measurable figure. For example, if late payments are the issue, how many invoices or what percentage are late? Without this, the business case cannot meet the 'baseline' criterion.

Why this matters: The baseline is essential for understanding the size of the problem and for tracking improvement later.

What to provide: Add a number that shows how big the issue is today — for instance, the proportion of invoices paid late in the period you mentioned or the exact count.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves attention, detailing what is wrong, where and since when, how big it is, and its costs. It must include a measurable baseline value.

Next, we'll define your project team: who leads, who sponsors, who owns the process, and who does the work. This is critical because a project needs people before it needs work. The champion clears obstacles, and the process owner keeps the result after the project ends — without them, a good fix fades.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

"Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project). Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers). Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process). Members: two billing clerks (know the work). Training: the clerks need a half-day on data collection before Measure."

Who leads the project? Who is the champion who can approve and clear obstacles? Who owns the process? Who else is on the team — and does anyone need training to take part fully?
reply.explanation: Define the team: who leads, sponsors, owns the process, and works on it. A project needs people before it needs work.

Next, we'll work on the Voice of the Customer (VOC). "Customers: client finance teams (external) and our credit control (internal). They need invoices that are correct and on time; the top complaint is wrong amounts. CTQs: invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines; invoice sent within 2 working days of the order."

Who are the customers of your process, and what do they need or complain about most? For each need, how would you measure that it is met?
reply.explanation: The Voice of the Customer (VOC) identifies who receives the process output, what they need, and how to measure those needs as Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs).

Next, we'll define your problem statement. The problem statement is the heart of the Define phase. It clearly describes the pain point your project is addressing, without naming any causes or solutions. This keeps everyone focused on solving the right problem and avoids jumping to conclusions.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

| Question | How it is formulated | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What | the defect, in one noun phrase | invoices returned for correction |
| Where | the process, the step(s) where it shows, and the place | UK billing, order to invoice — at "Generate invoice" |
| When | the period, or since when | January to June 2026 |
| Who | who is affected | client finance teams, credit control |
| Why | why it matters to them | wrong amounts delay payment and trust |
| How | how the defect shows up | clients return the invoice or dispute it |
| How much | the size, against a requirement | 12% of invoices, against 3% elsewhere |

Once answered, these combine into a single statement: *"From January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned by clients for correction — four times the 3% seen elsewhere — delaying payment for client finance teams and credit control."*

Next, we'll define your baseline estimate. The baseline estimate sets the starting point for your project — the primary metric that measures the defect you're solving, where it stands today, and the data it comes from. This is how you prove success later, so it must be clear and based on real data.

What it is: A metric is something you can count the same way twice. 'Invoice quality' isn't one — two people would score it differently. 'The share of invoices returned by collections for correction' is: you can point at any invoice and say yes or no.

Why it matters here: This is the number your whole project is judged on. Define sets it, Measure proves it, Control compares against it. If the definition shifts between phases, nothing downstream compares.

How to read it: A usable Define baseline has three parts: a number, the period it covers, and where it came from — a report, a log, a sample. 'About 12%' is a start; '12% of invoices returned, January to June, from the collections log' is something we can go and check.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

"Primary metric: invoice error rate — %, the share of invoices returned by clients for correction. Baseline: 12%, January to June 2026, from the collections log. It feeds the finance KPI days-sales-outstanding."

What is the one measure of the defect that will say whether the project succeeded? What unit is it in, what exactly does it count, and which business KPI does it feed? Where does it stand today — and which data is that number from?
reply.explanation: The baseline estimate sets the starting point for your project — the primary metric that measures the defect you're solving, where it stands today, and the data it comes from.

Next, we'll work on benefits analysis. This is where you quantify the value of solving the problem — what the gap costs today (the cost of poor quality), whether the gain is sustainable (every year) or one-off, when the money will be realised, and who in finance validates the figure.

What it is: The benefits analysis — the cost of the gap today (COPQ), whether the gain is sustainable or one-off, when the money will be realised, and who in finance validates the figure.

Why it matters: It establishes the value of the project in terms finance will accept. A figure a finance representative has checked is one the champion can defend.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

"Cost of the gap: about €11k a year in rework (4,200 invoices, 12% → 3%, about €30 each), from the savings calculation. Impact: sustainable — reduced cost every year. Realisation: from Q4 2026, about €2.7k a quarter. Finance contact: Priya Shah, management accountant." (Illustration)

Let's start with the cost of the gap. Cutting errors from 12% to 3% on about 4,200 invoices a year, at about €30 to put each one right, is roughly €11k a year. To calculate this for your project, we'll need two figures: the cost of one defect (with its currency) and the yearly volume. What does one late payment cost, and how many invoices do you handle a year?
reply.explanation: Benefits analysis quantifies the value of solving the problem in terms finance will accept.

The SIPOC maps your process as it runs today — Suppliers give Inputs; the Process, in four to eight main steps from start to end, turns them into Outputs, which go to Customers. Each step includes how long it takes (average, shortest, longest), how often it runs, and the problems the team sees there, with who said so. For the whole process, it includes the end-to-end lead time and how often it runs.

What it is: A SIPOC — a one-page, high-level map of the process as it runs today: Suppliers give Inputs; the Process, in four to eight main steps from start to end, turns them into Outputs, which go to Customers; and what is measured on those outputs. With it, how the process performs today: for each step, how long it takes (average, shortest and longest, with the unit), how often it runs, and the problems the team sees there and who said so; for the whole process, the end-to-end lead time and how often it runs. reply.answer:
Welcome to Measure. Quick recap of what Define locked in, so we're building on the same picture:

• **Problem:** From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices across our three hospital sites were paid after their 30-day terms. Suppliers chase us by phone and email, and some put us on stop, delaying stock for ward managers. The problem shows in the accounts payable process at the 'resolve mismatches' and 'approve invoice' steps, where invoices wait.
• **Baseline:** Late payment rate — 23%, from the AP ledger, January to June 2026.
• **Target:** Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.
• **Process (SIPOC):** Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites. Measuring: days from invoice receipt to payment release, and the share of invoices with a match exception.

Now, what Measure actually does: we expand that SIPOC into a detailed process map, decide what to collect and how, check the measurement itself can be trusted, confirm the process is behaving consistently, establish a real baseline, and prioritise which inputs are most likely driving the problem. You don't need to hold these in a fixed order in your head — I'll guide you — but here's the full menu so nothing's a surprise:

**Required (7)**
□ Detailed process map — timings, people, value vs waste per step
□ Data collection plan — what, how much, how often, who
□ Stability check — is the process behaving consistently?
□ Baseline — the current level, once we trust the data
□ Cause prioritisation — scoring what might be driving it
□ Vital few X's — the shortlist Analyse will test
□ Issues and barriers — what's in your way

**Recommended (3)**
□ Sigma level · □ Measurement system check · □ Secondary metrics

**Progress: 0 of 7 required complete**

We'll work through these roughly in the order above, and I'll flag the two recommended ones — the measurement system check and the sigma level — when we reach them, rather than saving them for the end. First up: expanding your Define map, because everything else attaches to it. Let me show you what that looks like.
reply.prompt: Let's start with the detailed process map. How many steps does your process have, and what happens at each? For each step, how long does it take at minimum, on average, and at worst? Who does it, and does it add value for the customer?

define_structured.business_case: Across our three hospital sites, 23% of supplier invoices were paid after their 30-day terms from January to June 2026. Late payments to our suppliers are costing us: we paid about £62,000 in late-payment interest and lost early-payment discounts last year, and three key medical suppliers put us on stop twice this year, which held up ward stock. To add detail: this is based on the AP ledger for January to June 2026, across all three hospital sites, and the finance director has agreed it.

define_structured.voc_summary: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late and not knowing when they will be paid; ward managers about deliveries being held. One more thing: suppliers also told us they cannot see the status of an invoice once it is submitted.

Suppliers chase us by phone and email, and some put us on stop, delaying stock for ward managers. The problem shows in the accounts payable process at the 'resolve mismatches' and 'approve invoice' steps, where invoices wait.
